title: Exact Hausdorff dimension of Liouville quantum gravity

current_openness: UNKNOWN (primary literature states open in 2025; no complete 2026 literature audit)
exact_statement: For each gamma in (0,2), determine d_gamma = the almost-sure Hausdorff dimension of (C,D_h), where D_h is the gamma-LQG metric of a whole-plane Gaussian free field h. The case gamma=sqrt(8/3) has d_gamma=4; the requested unsolved range is gamma in (0,2) excluding sqrt(8/3).

source_check.primary_problem: Gwynne and Miller, Existence and uniqueness of the Liouville quantum gravity metric for gamma in (0,2), arXiv:1905.00383v3, Problem 7.1 and equation (1.5), https://arxiv.org/html/1905.00383v3
source_check.dimension_identification: The same paper lines 128-130 states d_gamma is the metric Hausdorff dimension, citing Gwynne-Pfeffer; xi=gamma/d_gamma.
source_check.later_status: Borga and Gwynne, Directed distances in bipolar-oriented triangulations, arXiv:2510.26123v1, introduction lines 118-119, states d_gamma unknown away from sqrt(8/3), https://arxiv.org/html/2510.26123v1
source_check.qualification: 2018 Ding-Gwynne predates the metric construction and only expected equality of its exponent with metric dimension; do not treat its old conjectural phrasing as a remaining bridge after Gwynne-Pfeffer.

primary_quote: Compute the exponent d_gamma appearing in (1.5), which is the Hausdorff dimension of C with respect to the gamma-LQG metric.

prior_attempt_correction: The D0049-A001 intake equation d_gamma=2Q/xi is false: gamma=sqrt(8/3), Q=5/sqrt(6), xi=1/sqrt(6) would yield 10 rather than the known 4. Correct xi=gamma/d_gamma is in Gwynne-Miller equation (1.5).
